pages.text: Every harvest season, Bawa watched his mother’s tomatoes soften and rot behind the market shed. Whenever a daytime power cut shut down the traders’ small cold room, they had to sell cheaply before everything spoiled. “Farmers sweat for months, and then post-harvest loss eats their profit,” Naana said. She pointed up. “Meanwhile the sun beats on that zinc roof all afternoon.” So when a solar technician, Engineer Maame Efua, arrived to install a solar-powered cold room for the market cooperative, the three friends asked to follow the energy at every stage.

She pointed up.

“Meanwhile the sun beats on that zinc roof all afternoon.” So when a solar technician, Engineer Maame Efua, arrived to install a solar-powered cold room for the market cooperative, the three friends asked to follow the energy at every stage.
pages.alt: Outside a sunny Ghanaian market cooperative shed, crates of red tomatoes sit in shade while JHS students watch Engineer Maame Efua unload gleaming blue-black solar panels beside the corrugated roof.

pages.text: Engineer Maame Efua sketched a block diagram in chalk. “First, do not confuse two things,” she said. “A solar water heater uses sunlight to heat water. These are photovoltaic panels, or PV for short. Their silicon cells change light energy directly into electrical energy, as direct current (DC). The panels must be tilted towards the sun and kept clean. Harmattan dust or bird droppings block the light. From the panels, the current flows to a charge controller, which protects the batteries from overcharging. Then an inverter changes the DC into 230-volt alternating current (AC), the kind that runs the cold-room motor.”

pages.alt: Clear, labelled four-stage gouache diagram alongside the market wall: (1) Angled Solar PV Panels, (2) Charge Controller, (3) Battery Bank, and (4) Inverter powering a cold room.

pages.text: Edem wrote the energy chain in his notebook. “So in bright sunshine, the photovoltaic cells change light energy into electrical energy. Some runs the cold room at once. The rest is stored in the batteries as chemical energy and changed back into electrical energy after sunset.” “Exactly,” said Engineer Maame Efua, impressed. “Compare that with a petrol generator. It gives off carbon monoxide and soot, it is noisy, and it needs fuel every single day. A solar system costs a lot to install. After that the sunshine is free. But it still needs care, and one day the batteries must be replaced.”

pages.text: In Social Studies, Edem and Bawa studied how the cooperative paid for it all. Twenty-five market women had saved together every week through their credit union. Now each trader paid a small cooling fee per crate. The fees went into a separate account for cleaning the panels and, one day, replacing the batteries. “This is entrepreneurship,” their teacher said. “They saw a real need and organised to meet it. Cutting post-harvest loss raises incomes for farmers and traders and keeps food prices steadier for families. It also creates skilled jobs for technicians like Maame Efua.”

pages.text: In RME, the class talked about honest work. “Some young people are tempted by internet fraud or betting, because they think skilled work is too slow,” Naana said. “But Christians are taught that hard work brings dignity, and that whoever is faithful with a little can be trusted with much. Islam honours halal earnings: money gained through honest labour, fair weights, and kept promises. And our elders praise adwuma pa—good, honest work.” Edem thought of the cooperative’s ledger. “That is why the women record every cedi,” he said. “Trust is part of the business.”

pages.alt: Naana, Bawa, and Edem in Career Technology aprons assembling a small low-voltage 6-volt solar-LED lantern kit on their workbench while Engineer Maame Efua coaches them.

pages.text: The project gave the Science and Career Technology Club an idea. Under their teacher’s supervision, the members built a safe 6-volt solar lantern for the reading corner of the school library. They wrote a rota for checking the small panel for dust and wiping it, with an adult, when it was cool. At the market, Bawa’s mother was now selling firm, fresh tomatoes three days after harvest. Far fewer crates were going to waste. The three friends could see it clearly: science, enterprise, and honest character had turned ordinary sunlight into lasting gain.

activities.question: What do the charge controller and the inverter do in a solar PV system?
options: The inverter makes diesel fuel, while the charge controller heats water
The controller guards batteries; the inverter turns DC into 230 V AC power
Both devices block electrons completely so batteries never store chemical energy

activities.question: Which sequence correctly traces the energy transformations when solar panels charge a battery by day to run a light at night?
options: Chemical energy in dust → Heat energy → Magnetic energy
Nuclear energy in glass → Sound energy → Kinetic energy → Potential energy
Light energy → Electrical energy → Chemical energy → Electrical energy

activities.question: How does solar-powered cold storage strengthen Ghana’s agricultural economy?
options: It cuts crop loss, stabilizes trader incomes, and saves generator fuel costs
It forces farmers to throw away half their harvest on day one
It increases exhaust smoke and noise inside food markets

activities.question: Apply it: A solar cold room is losing power during Harmattan. What is the best first step?
options: Ask students to open the high-voltage inverter cabinet
Have a certified technician inspect panels, wiring, and battery safety
Assume solar panels cannot work during Harmattan

activities.prompt: Put the flow of energy in a solar cold-room system in the correct order, from sunlight to appliance.
items: Solar PV cells on the clean rooftop absorb sunlight and produce DC power.
A charge controller regulates DC voltage to safeguard storage batteries.
Chemical energy is stored in batteries to maintain steady backup power.
An inverter transforms DC into 230 V AC to run the cold-room refrigeration.

activities.definition: Relating to the direct conversion of light energy into electrical energy using semiconductor materials such as silicon.
distractors: Generating power by burning diesel fuel inside a noisy generator engine
Preserving fresh tomatoes by boiling them in concentrated salt solution

glossary.definition: Technology (PV) in which semiconductor solar cells convert sunlight directly into direct-current (DC) electricity.
Electric current (DC) in which charges flow steadily in one direction, as produced by solar cells and batteries.
An electronic device that converts direct current (DC) from solar panels or batteries into alternating current (AC) for standard appliances.
The spoilage, damage, or waste of farm produce between harvesting and human consumption due to poor storage, transport, or processing.
Identifying a real community need, organising resources responsibly, and bearing calculated risk to create sustainable value.
